questions.question_text: Which statement about the sample mean $\bar{X}$ is correct?

options.text: $\bar{X}$ is a random variable, because its value depends on which sample happens to be drawn.
$\bar{X}$ is a random variable, because the population mean $\mu$ changes from sample to sample.
options.why: Gives the right classification for the wrong reason; $\mu$ is a fixed parameter and never changes.

options.text: $\bar{X}$ is a constant, because every sample used has the same size $n$.
options.why: Confuses a fixed sample size with a fixed sample mean; equal-sized samples still contain different items.

options.text: $\bar{X}$ is a constant, because it always takes the value $\mu$.
options.why: Confuses $E(\bar{X})=\mu$ with $\bar{X}=\mu$; the mean of the distribution is $\mu$, not every value of it.

questions.solution_text:
A different sample gives a different value of $\bar{X}$, and which sample is drawn is decided by chance.
A quantity whose value is decided by chance is a random variable.

questions.question_text: A population consists of the three values $3$, $7$ and $10$. Samples of size $2$ are taken with replacement and the order is recorded. Find $P(\bar{X}=5)$.

options.why: Counted the pair $3$ and $7$ once although both orders, $(3,7)$ and $(7,3)$, are separate samples.
Used the number of population values, $3$, as the denominator instead of the $9$ possible samples.
Counted only one pair and divided by the $3$ population values, combining both errors.

questions.solution_text:
There are $3\times3=9$ equally likely ordered samples.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 3 & 7 & 10 \\ \hline 3 & 3 & 5 & 6.5 \\ 7 & 5 & 7 & 8.5 \\ 10 & 6.5 & 8.5 & 10 \end{array}$
A mean of $5$ occurs for $(3,7)$ and $(7,3)$.
$P(\bar{X}=5)=\frac{2}{9}$

questions.question_text: A population consists of the three values $5$, $9$ and $16$. Samples of size $2$ are taken with replacement. Find $E(\bar{X})$.

options.why: Divided the population mean by the sample size $2$; the centre of the sampling distribution does not shrink.
Multiplied the population mean by the sample size $2$, treating $\bar{X}$ as a sample total.
Added the population values but never divided by $3$ to get the population mean.

questions.solution_text:
$\mu=\frac{5+9+16}{3}$
$=\frac{30}{3}$
$=10$
The mean of every possible sample mean equals the population mean.
$E(\bar{X})=10$

questions.question_text:
The sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \bar{x} & 20 & 21 & 22 & 23 & 24 \\ \hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x}) & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.30 & 0.25 & 0.10 \end{array}$
Find $P(\bar{X}\ge 23)$.

options.why: Used only the bar at $\bar{x}=23$ and left out $\bar{x}=24$.
Read the inequality as $\bar{X}>23$ and used only $\bar{x}=24$.
Gave the complement $1-0.35$, which is $P(\bar{X}<23)$.
Used only the bar at $\bar{x}=5$ and left out $\bar{x}=4$.
Used only the bar at $\bar{x}=4$, reading the inequality as $\bar{X}<5$.
Gave the complement $1-0.25$, which is $P(\bar{X}>5)$.

questions.solution_text:
The bars at $\bar{x}=4$ and $\bar{x}=5$ have heights $0.05$ and $0.20$.
$P(\bar{X}\le 5)=0.05+0.20$
$=0.25$

questions.question_text: A population consists of the values $1$, $5$, $9$ and $13$. Samples of size $3$ are taken without replacement. Which statement compares the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ with the population?

options.text: $\bar{X}$ has the same mean as the population and a smaller range.
$\bar{X}$ has the same mean as the population and the same range.
options.why: Misses that a sample of $3$ can never average as low as $1$ or as high as $13$.

options.text: $\bar{X}$ has a smaller mean than the population and a smaller range.
options.why: Assumes averaging shrinks the centre as well as the spread; $E(\bar{X})=\mu$ always.

options.text: $\bar{X}$ has a smaller mean than the population and the same range.
options.why: Shrinks the wrong feature: the centre is unchanged and it is the spread that narrows.

questions.solution_text:
The mean of every possible sample mean equals the population mean, so the centres agree.
The smallest possible mean is $\frac{1+5+9}{3}=5$ and the largest is $\frac{5+9+13}{3}=9$.
The range of $\bar{X}$ is $4$, while the population range is $12$.

questions.question_text: A population consists of the four values $3$, $5$, $8$ and $12$. Samples of size $2$ are taken without replacement. Find $P(\bar{X}=4)$.

options.why: Counted the two orders of each pair, although order is not recorded when the sample is a set of two items.
Used the $16$ ordered samples available with replacement instead of the $6$ available without it.
Used the number of population values, $4$, as the number of possible samples.

questions.question_text:
Samples of size $2$ are taken with replacement from a population of three values, and the resulting sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \bar{x} & 5 & 9 & 13 & 17 & 21 \\ \hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x}) & \frac{1}{9} & \frac{2}{9} & \frac{3}{9} & \frac{2}{9} & \frac{1}{9} \end{array}$
Find the three population values.

options.why: Took the three smallest possible sample means as the population, ignoring that $17$ and $21$ must also be reachable.
Took the three most likely sample means, but the extreme means $5$ and $21$ can only arise from population values.
Halved each of $5$, $13$ and $21$, treating the sample mean as needing to be undone by dividing by $2$.

questions.solution_text:
A mean of $5$ can only come from choosing the smallest value twice, so the smallest value is $5$.
A mean of $21$ can only come from choosing the largest value twice, so the largest value is $21$.
The middle value $a$ gives $\bar{x}=a$ when chosen twice, and the remaining mean with probability $\frac{3}{9}$ is $13$.
$a=13$
The population values are $5$, $13$ and $21$.
